uncited: This method constructs a sparse octree from a list of active leaf nodes (sorted by Morton code) in a bottom-up, breadth-first manner.

It solves the problem of efficiently linking hierarchical parent-child relationships and establishing spatial adjacency (specifically x-neighbor pointers) without requiring global sorting or complex tree traversal algorithms.
**Inputs:** A list of active level-0 nodes (`ActNodes1`), where each entry contains a Morton code and potentially payload data.
**Outputs:** A fully linked octree structure with parent-child pointers and x-neighbor pointers for all levels up to a specified top level $n$.
Each element contains a `morton_code` (integer) and `payload`.
Size is $8 \times \text{length}(ActNodes1)$.
Size is $8 \times N_{a2}$, where $N_{a2}$ is the number of active nodes at the next level.
Allocate `Nodes0` with size $8 \times \text{length}(ActNodes1)$.
Set x-neighbor pointers between adjacent nodes within `Nodes0` that share the same parent.
Specifically, nodes at indices $8i$ and $8i+1$, $8i+2$ and $8i+3$, etc., are linked if they are siblings.
*   Check if `ActNodes1[i+1]` has a different level-1 parent than `ActNodes1[i]`.
This is determined by comparing the Morton codes (specifically, checking if the higher-order bits defining the parent differ).
*   Write `1` to `Flag1[i]` if the parent is different, `0` otherwise.
*   Set `Flag1[last] = 1` to ensure the last node is counted as a boundary.
Perform an exclusive scan (prefix sum) on `Flag1` to produce `ParentIndex1`.
*   $N_{a2} = \text{ParentIndex1}[\text{last}] + 1$.
This is the number of active nodes at the next level (level 1).
Allocate `Nodes1` with size $8 \times N_{a2}$.
*   Set the parent pointer of `Nodes0[8*i]` (the first child of the $i$-th active node) to `Nodes1[j]`.
*   Establish child pointers in `Nodes1[j]` pointing to the 8 children in `Nodes0` starting at index $8*i$.
*   Strip the three least significant bits from each Morton code in `ActNodes1` (integer division by 8 or bitwise right shift by 3).
*   Compact the list using `Flag1` and `ParentIndex1` to remove duplicates (since multiple children map to the same parent).
The compacted list contains unique parent Morton codes.
Repeat steps 1-6 using `ActNodes2` as the input for the next level.
Continue this process for all remaining levels.
Stop the iterative construction two levels below the theoretical root node (level $n$).
At this top level $n$, all possible nodes are created explicitly because the tree is dense enough at the top.
Establish x-neighbor pointers for all adjacent nodes at this level.
*   Propagate x-neighbor pointers from nodes in level $i$ to their children in level $i-1$.
*   For adjacent nodes in level $i-1$ that have *different* parents, link them via x-neighbor pointers.
This ensures spatial continuity across parent boundaries.
*   **Time Complexity:** Linear with respect to the number of active leaf nodes $N$, assuming the Morton code sorting is already done.
The scan and pointer establishment are $O(N)$.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(N)$ for storing the tree nodes.
The algorithm requires temporary buffers (`Flag1`, `ParentIndex1`) proportional to the number of active nodes at each level.
Avoids complex tree balancing or recursive descent.
Only maintains x-neighbor adjacency, which may be insufficient for algorithms requiring full 26-neighbor connectivity.
*   **When to use:** When constructing sparse octrees from voxelized data or point clouds where x-neighbor traversal is sufficient (e.g., certain ray marching or surface reconstruction algorithms).
It shares similarities with the approach by Zhou et al. [2010], proceeding bottom-up in a breadth-first fashion using Morton ordering.
The main differences are in the stored payload (volumetric vs. point cloud) and the adjacency information maintained (x-neighbor vs. all 26 neighbors).
